facts.text: A performance baseline is a careful measurement of the existing warning-only system's performance, made before judging the new braking system so that improvement has a reference.
facts.quote: A performance baseline is a careful measurement of how well the existing warning-only system performs, made before the new braking system is judged

facts.text: Chapter 7 defines the warning-system baseline's unit of analysis as an encounter, not a frame: machine A approaches object B under scenario C while the object occupies or approaches a defined risk region.
facts.quote: The unit of analysis is the encounter, not the frame: "machine A approached object B under scenario C while the object occupied or approached a defined risk region".

facts.text: Each baseline encounter carries factors for machine model and configuration, sensor mounting, object class, direction, speed, grade, surface, load, weather, light, dust and site type.
facts.quote: Each encounter carries its factors: machine model and configuration, sensor mounting, object class, direction, speed, grade, surface, load, weather, light, dust and site type.

facts.text: The baseline encounter's risk region should follow ISO 21815-3, the International Organization for Standardization standard on collision warning risk areas for earth-moving machinery, rather than an arbitrary sensor range.
facts.quote: The risk region should follow ISO 21815-3 (a standard from the International Organization for Standardization on collision warning risk areas for earth-moving machinery), not an arbitrary sensor range

facts.text: Baseline detection measures should include detection probability per encounter by object class (standing, crouching or lying worker, light vehicle, or another machine), distance band, bearing and condition, plus first-detection distance and time and missed encounters. Reporting should use curves or bins rather than a fleet-wide average that hides weak conditions.
facts.quote: plus first-detection distance and time and missed encounters, reported as curves or bins rather than one fleet-wide average that hides weak conditions.

facts.text: Baseline warning rates should be measured per operating hour and split into false warnings (no object), nuisance warnings (a real object without risk, such as the machine's own tires or a berm), and correct warnings, because these represent different engineering problems.
facts.quote: False and nuisance warnings: per operating hour, split into false (no object), nuisance (a real object but no risk, such as the machine's own tires or a berm) and correct, because these are different engineering problems.

facts.text: Recommended baseline warning-timing measures are time to collision or distance at first warning, detection latency, warning duration and repeated warnings.
facts.quote: Warning timing: time to collision or distance at first warning, detection latency, warning duration and repeated warnings.

facts.text: Baseline availability measures should include time in normal, degraded, inhibited and fault states; detection rates measured only while the system is available can hide unavailability.
facts.quote: Availability: time in normal, degraded, inhibited and fault states, since an impressive detection rate measured only while "available" can hide unavailability

facts.text: The established method for measuring the warning-system baseline without driving the machine is replaying recorded raw sensor logs against independent ground truth.
facts.quote: The established way to measure all this without driving the machine is to replay recorded raw sensor logs against an independent ground truth.

facts.text: Baseline quality depends on what was recorded; treating the detector's own output as ground truth is circular because missed objects disappear from both predictions and the supposed truth.
facts.quote: The baseline is only as good as what was recorded, and using the detector's own output as truth is circular: objects it missed vanish from both the prediction and the "truth".

facts.text: The booklet recommends starting raw sensor recording in October 2026 rather than waiting for the prototype to arrive.
facts.quote: That is why the booklet says recording must start now, in October 2026, not when the prototype arrives.

facts.text: Brake-request time, achieved deceleration, stopping distance and false interventions cannot be measured on the old warning-only system; braking-function measures must instead be judged against new requirements.
facts.quote: Measures of the braking function itself (brake-request time, achieved deceleration, stopping distance, false interventions) cannot be measured on the old system and are judged against new requirements instead

facts.text: The baseline sample-size guidance calls for 59 consecutive successful encounters per stratum for a 95 percent detection claim and 299 for a 99 percent detection claim.
facts.quote: 59 consecutive successful encounters per stratum for 95 percent detection, 299 for 99 percent

facts.text: The baseline sample-size guidance calls for 30 failure-free hours per condition to show fewer than 0.1 false alarms per hour.
facts.quote: 30 failure-free hours per condition to show fewer than 0.1 false alarms per hour.

facts.text: No standard sets the baseline sample-size figures of 59 or 299 successful encounters per stratum or 30 failure-free hours per condition.
The warning-system baseline supplies the field distribution used to weight every rate claim and is the program's only source of real exposure and false-alarm data.
facts.quote: The baseline is also the source of the field distribution that every rate claim must be weighted by, and the only real exposure and false-alarm data the program will have.

facts.text: Chapter 7 calls parallel recording on current machines the single most valuable pre-hardware action for the program.
facts.quote: Chapter 7 calls parallel recording on current machines "the single most valuable pre-hardware action"
